functions.description: Create one or more files. Request shape: {"files": [{"path": "...", "content": "..."}]}. Per-file `overwrite` and `parents` flags; non-accessible paths return C211. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*.

Remove one or more paths. Request shape: {"paths": ["..."]}. Directories need `recursive: true`; missing paths are idempotent successes; recursive removal refuses to descend through non-accessible entries. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*.

Report the coder access contract: the effective mode (jailed = paths confined to the allowed roots; unjailed = deny-only, absolute paths anywhere on the host, roots anchor relative paths only), canonical allowed roots (primary first), the session_root that relative paths actually anchor against when the session is scoped (it overrides primary_root and may sit outside every allowed root), per-file size caps, response budgets (max_output_bytes, batch_read_budget_bytes, search_response_budget_bytes), listing/search limits, the non-accessible glob patterns, and the default_exclude_globs noise filter applied by tree/search. Call this FIRST when unsure where coder may read or write, or when a path was rejected — in jailed mode, paths outside every allowed root need the shell worker's shell::fs::* instead.

Paginated single-folder listing, sorted by name. Entries carry only `name`; derive an entry's absolute path as the response's `path` + '/' + name. Non-accessible entries are still listed with a `non_accessible: true` flag. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*.

Move or rename one or more paths inside the jail. Request shape: {"files": [{"from": "...", "to": "..."}]}. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*. Per-entry `overwrite` and `parents` flags. Same-root moves use a per-file-atomic rename; cross-root moves use copy+delete (files only — cross-root directory moves are unsupported, move files individually). Copy+delete is rollback-safe: if source deletion fails after a successful copy the copy is removed and the error names the failure; if rollback also fails the error names both states for manual cleanup.

Read a file window-first: probe with stat: true (size/mtime/mode plus total_lines, no content), then fetch just the lines you need with line_from/line_to (1-based, inclusive) — windows keep files larger than max_read_bytes readable window by window, with more_lines/total_lines reporting what remains. numbered: true prefixes each line with its absolute 1-based file line number, matching coder::update-file's line ops exactly. Full reads are budgeted by max_output_bytes (default 128 KiB; per-call override clamped to max_read_bytes) — an over-budget full read fails with a C218 carrying the file's size, line count, and the window/stat recovery calls. Batch mode: pass paths[] (XOR path) to read multiple files in one call — entries are processed in request order against batch_read_budget_bytes, measured in bytes of returned content (after UTF-8 sanitization); per-entry errors (C211/C218) leave other entries unaffected. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*. Non-accessible paths return C211.

Search file contents and/or paths. Supports literal or regex queries with include/exclude globs; non-accessible files are excluded from both content and path results. Only the FIRST match on each line is reported (one content match per matching line). Optional context_lines_before/context_lines_after (max 10) attach surrounding lines to each content match so many edits can go straight to coder::update-file with no read in between. Noise paths matching default_exclude_globs (.git, node_modules, target, … — coder::info lists them) are skipped by default; pass use_default_excludes: false to search inside them. Files larger than max_read_bytes are silently skipped during content scanning. Results are capped by max_matches AND a response byte budget (search_response_budget_bytes); when truncated is true, refine the query or add include_globs rather than paginate. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*.

Recursive directory snapshot bounded by `max_depth` and a `per_folder_limit`. Slim wire shape: nodes carry only `name` — the root node's path IS the response's top-level `path`; derive any child's path as parent path + '/' + name. Folders that hit the limit are flagged `truncated` and the caller is pointed at coder::list-folder for pagination. Noise directories matching default_exclude_globs (.git, node_modules, target, … — coder::info lists them) appear as childless `truncated` stubs; pass use_default_excludes: false to descend into them. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*.

Apply batched line-oriented and regex edits across one or more files. Request shape: {"files": [{"path": "...", "ops": [...]}]}. Line ops: { op: 'insert', at_line, content } | { op: 'remove', from_line, to_line } | { op: 'update_lines', from_line, to_line, content } — 1-based, inclusive, applied bottom-up. Regex op: { op: 'replace', pattern, replacement, ignore_case?, dot_matches_newline?, expect_matches? } runs on the file body after line ops. Replace large regions WITHOUT quoting them: two short anchors joined by .*? with dot_matches_newline: true — always prefer wildcards over pasting the block into the pattern. expect_matches: 1 turns a silent multi-site clobber into a safe pre-write C210; expect_matches: 0 asserts absence. In `replacement`, $1/${name} are capture references and a literal $ must be written $$ (JS/TS template literals: `Hello, $${name}!`); undefined references fail pre-write with C210. Each file commits atomically via temp + rename. On success each applied line op returns a bounded post-apply echo (±2 context lines); regex replace ops return up to 5 per-match-site echoes (first + last line of each replaced region, inner lines elided) — verify from the echoes instead of re-reading the file. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*.
Read a configuration by id. Expands ${VAR:default} placeholders against the live process env unless raw=true is passed.
List every registered configuration with id, name, description, and schema. Sorted by id; never returns the stored value.

Register a configuration id with a name, description, and JSON Schema. Idempotent — re-registering replaces metadata and (when initial_value is provided) the value. Validates initial_value against the schema.
Retrieve the schema, name, and description for a configuration id. Mirrors a single entry from configuration::list.
Replace the value of an already-registered configuration. Validates the value against the registered JSON Schema and emits a configuration:updated event.
Estimate token usage for a set of messages (+ optional invocation schemas / system prompt) vs a model.
Replace verbose function outputs with placeholders without summarising. A cheaper first pass before compaction.
Internal: reload cron configuration from the authoritative store on change.
Open an interactive transaction; returns a handle to use with transactionQuery/transactionExecute/commitTransaction/rollbackTransaction.

Read a table page by page with typed filters and sorts, without writing SQL. Filters are structured (column, op, value) and compile to a parameterised WHERE for the driver in hand; the total honours the same filters. Use an equality filter at page_size 1 to follow a foreign key.

Profile a table's columns. Reads the planner's own statistics by default, which is free and approximate; `exact` runs real aggregates and scans the table. To profile rows you already hold, pipe a browseTable result through the fp worker instead.
Commit and finalize an interactive transaction.
Delete a saved query by id or by name.

Describe every table at once — the same shape as describeTable, but one catalog query per aspect across the whole database instead of one call per table. Use this to reason about relationships; set include_indexes only when you need them.

Describe one table or view: columns with type, nullability, default, primary-key membership and foreign-key target; plus indexes and a planner row estimate. Foreign keys are structured (schema, table, column), not a joined string.
Run a write statement (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL).
Run an ordered batch of SQL statements atomically (bare strings or {sql, params} objects); rolls back on first failure.

Return a statement's query plan as a tree with per-node costs, row estimates and warnings, instead of the driver's raw text. `analyze` collects real timings by RUNNING the statement, so it defaults to false and is refused for anything that is not a single read.

How a table is laid out for reading: column widths, hidden columns and column order. Stored in the state worker rather than a browser, so it survives a restart and any caller can set it up for someone else.

Live pool occupancy plus active queries, table sizes, blocking locks and cache hit ratio. Each section reports separately as available, unsupported or denied, so a driver gap or a restricted role is never mistaken for an empty result.

Recent queries run against a database, newest first. Best effort — recording never blocks or fails a query, so this is a convenience rather than an audit log. For an audit trail bind database::row-changed.
List all configured databases with connection details (driver, credential-redacted URL, pool settings, TLS mode). Config only — no health checks or live pool statistics.
List the saved queries for a database, sorted by name.
List every table and view in a database, with its kind and (on postgres) its schema. Reads the driver's own catalog, so no dialect-specific SQL is needed from the caller.
Internal: reload connection pools from the authoritative configuration when it changes.
Prepare a parameterized statement once.
Run a read-only SQL query and return the result rows.
Rollback and finalize an interactive transaction.
Run a previously-prepared handle.
Save a named query against a database. Stored in the state worker, so it survives restarts and an agent can save one for a human to find in the console. Saving under an existing name replaces it.

Replace the stored layout for a table. Widths are clamped to a usable range; columns the table no longer has are kept rather than rejected, so a rename degrades to a missing width instead of an error.

Lay out the schema as a diagram: positioned table nodes and routed foreign-key edges, plus the hub degree of each table, the isolated tables, and the remaining edge crossings. Reads the whole catalog in a handful of queries rather than one per table.
Terminate a backend session, or cancel just its running statement with `cancel_only`. Takes an id from database::health. Separate from health because it is a write.
Probe a candidate database config (url + optional tls) with one throwaway connection, without touching configured pools. Reports ok/driver/latency/server version; failures are data, not errors.
Run a sequence of statements atomically.
Run a write statement inside an interactive transaction. BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK are rejected; use commit/rollbackTransaction.
Run a read-only SQL query inside an interactive transaction.
Full detail for one engine function: schemas, owning worker, and registered triggers that target it. Proxies to the engine's native engine::functions::info for the core data.
Fetch one filesystem-backed prompt by name. Returns the raw markdown body plus name, description, and modified_at — no envelope, no templating.
List filesystem-backed prompts (name, description, modified_at) from skills_folder.

Overwrite one EXISTING filesystem-backed prompt with new full-file markdown content. The frontmatter must keep a non-empty `description` (and a valid `name` when it declares one) — the same rules the scanner enforces, so an update can never produce a file the next directory::prompts::list would skip. The write is atomic and fans out directory::prompts::on-change with { op: "update" }. Returns the prompt's effective name after the write (frontmatter `name:` wins over the file stem).

Fetch full registry metadata for one worker: worker envelope (same core fields as the engine's `engine::workers::list` row shape, plus registry-only `type` / `config` / `supported_targets` / `total_downloads` / `dependencies` / `image`), readme, full API reference (functions + triggers schemas), and the tree of skill / prompt file paths fetched from the registry's /w/{slug}/skills endpoint. Pass either `version` or `tag` (defaults to tag="latest"). Results are cached for `registry_cache_ttl_ms`.

List workers from the public registry (api.workers.iii.dev). Optional free-text `search` is matched fuzzily by the registry; omit it to browse by `total_downloads DESC`. Pagination is cursor-based with a server-authored page size — pass back `pagination.next_cursor` as `cursor` to fetch the next page. Shares the core `name` / `description` / `version` fields with the engine's `engine::workers::list`. Results are cached for `registry_cache_ttl_ms` (default 60s).

Download skills + prompts into skills_folder from EITHER source. Prefer the explicit directory::skills::download_from_registry / directory::skills::download_from_repo, whose schemas can't be mixed up. Pass {repo, skill, branch?} to clone one skill folder from a GitHub repo (branch defaults to "main"), or {worker, version?|tag?} to pull from the workers registry (tag defaults to "latest"). Specify exactly ONE source set. Files in the destination namespace are overwritten file-by-file.

Download one worker's skills + prompts from the workers registry into skills_folder. `worker` is required; pass either `version` (exact semver) OR `tag` (e.g. "latest", the default when both are omitted), not both. Files in the destination namespace are overwritten file-by-file. A missing worker returns a `D310 not_found` naming the next function to call. To pull from a GitHub repo instead, use directory::skills::download_from_repo.

Download one skill folder from a GitHub repo into skills_folder. `repo` (the repo URL) and `skill` (the subfolder under `skills/`, which also names the destination namespace) are required; `branch` defaults to "main". The repo URL is validated (https / ssh / git@ only). To pull a published worker instead, use directory::skills::download_from_registry.

Fetch one filesystem-backed skill by id and return its raw markdown body plus id, title, type, function_id, and modified_at. A worker overview is addressed by the bare worker name (e.g. "iii-sandbox") — that is the id `list`/`index` hand back. Input is forgiving: "iii-sandbox/index", "iii-sandbox/SKILL.md", a trailing ".md", and an iii:// prefix all resolve to the same overview; and if the exact id misses, the worker name is matched case-insensitively as a substring ("sandbox" finds "iii-sandbox"). `title` prefers frontmatter `title:` over the body H1; `type` is the frontmatter `type:`. There is no `description` field here (the body already opens with that paragraph) — use directory::skills::list for the teaser-only view. On a miss you get a `D110 not_found` message naming the closest ids and the next function to call.

Render a per-WORKER overview: one short markdown block per installed worker (each worker's root overview doc `<ns>/index`, whether or not it declares frontmatter `type: index`). Each block is a `## <worker title>` heading, the first paragraph of that worker's overview, and a `directory::skills::get` call to read the full reference. Token-light by design and intended for system-prompt injection; for individual per-SKILL rows call directory::skills::list.

List skills as one row PER SKILL (id, title, type, function_id, description, bytes, modified_at) from skills_folder — use this when you need individual skill ids. A worker overview row's `id` is the bare worker name (e.g. `iii-sandbox`); pass it straight to directory::skills::get. For a per-WORKER overview instead, call directory::skills::index. Filters: `search` (case-insens. substring vs id+title+description), `prefix` (worker-namespace prefix; matches the overview row and its sub-skills), `type` (exact frontmatter type match). Pass `include_description: false` for token-light id+title+type rows (default: descriptions included). `title` prefers frontmatter `title:` over the body H1. Each row's `function_id` is the callable bus id (e.g. `sandbox::create`) — pass THAT to agent_trigger, not the row's `id` (which is a documentation address).

Overwrite one EXISTING filesystem-backed skill with new full-file markdown content (frontmatter block included — pass back the `raw` field from directory::skills::get { raw: true }, edited). Accepts the same id forms as `get`. Never creates files (use directory::skills::download to materialize a bundle). Content is validated against the read invariants (size cap, non-empty body after frontmatter); the write is atomic and fans out directory::skills::on-change with { op: "update" }.
Browse DLQ messages
List DLQ topics with counts
Internal provider for TriggerAction::Enqueue
List all queue topics
Get stats for a queue topic

Remove null elements from an array (lodash _.compact, null-only: 0, false and "" are KEPT so plucked data survives): { value }. Pairs with fp::map, whose sporadic misses become null. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Trigger-binding guard: compare a JSON pointer inside the fired event and answer the condition contract ({ decision: "allow" | "skip", reason }). Config is { path?, op, to?, negate? } with the fp::when ops (==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, exists, not_empty); a pointer that resolves to nothing SKIPS rather than erroring, so "not there yet" is an ordinary answer. Use it as a binding's `conditions` entry so a reaction fires only on events that matter — it is not a fan-in gate (that is state::barrier), it filters one event at a time.

Count array elements per plucked key (lodash _.countBy): { value, path: "/writer" } -> { "<key>": <count> } (`""` counts by the element itself). Same key rules as fp::groupBy. Pair with fp::groupBy + fp::sum for a per-key total. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Skip the first n elements of an array or the first n characters of a string (lodash _.drop): { value, n }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Keep array elements whose properties equal a partial object (lodash _.filter with a matches iteratee): { value, matches: { status: "active" } }. matches is a partial OBJECT (never a bare string/number) and only object elements can match. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Flatten an array one level (lodash _.flatten): [1,[2],[[3]]] -> [1,2,[3]]. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Extract the single value at a JSON pointer (lodash _.get): { value, path: "/content" }. A miss names the keys that were available. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Extract the value at a JSON pointer, or `default` when the path misses (lodash fp.getOr): { value, path, default }. A stored null is a hit, not a miss. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Bucket array elements by a plucked key (lodash _.groupBy): { value, path: "/writer" } -> { "<key>": [element, ...] } (`""` groups by the element itself). Keys must be a string, number, or boolean; a null or container key errors rather than collapsing distinct groups into one bucket. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Join array elements into one string (lodash _.join): { value, separator } (separator defaults to ","). Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Pluck the value at a JSON pointer from each array element (lodash _.map with a property iteratee): { value, path: "/id" }. Sporadic misses become null (fp::compact drops them), but a path matching NO element errors — pointers pluck stored fields, not computed properties like /length (fp::size counts). Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Largest number in an array (lodash _.max/_.maxBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" }. Deviates from lodash _.maxBy: returns the NUMBER, not the element holding it, so a fp::when guard can compare it directly. An empty array errors. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Arithmetic mean of an array of numbers (lodash _.mean/_.meanBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/score" }. Deviates from lodash: an EMPTY array errors instead of yielding NaN, which would thread garbage into the next step. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Smallest number in an array (lodash _.min/_.minBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" }. Deviates from lodash _.minBy: returns the NUMBER, not the element holding it, so a fp::when guard can compare it directly. An empty array errors. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Element at index n; negative n counts from the end (lodash _.nth): { value, n: -1 } is the last element. Out of bounds errors naming the length. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Drop top-level keys from an object (lodash _.omit): { value, paths: ["a","b"] }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Subset an object by top-level keys (lodash _.pick): { value, paths: ["a","b"] } -> {a, b}; missing keys are omitted. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Run a short worker-side pipeline in one call: each step triggers a function and its result lands in the next step's payload at `into` (default "/value") — large values flow worker→worker and never enter the chat. fp::* transform steps (get/pick/omit/take/drop/map/filter/split/join/uniq/size/compact/nth/getOr/flatten/sortBy/reverse/when, lodash semantics) run inline and thread the transformed value itself — the {value} wrapper they return when called directly never appears between steps. A failing fp::when guard STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step runs only when its condition holds. The FIRST step receives no threaded value: start with a producing function (a fetch, a state::get) or seed a leading transform via payload.value. Example: fetch an article and persist it trimmed: through=[{function:'scrapling::fetch', payload:{url,format:'markdown'}}, {function:'fp::get', payload:{path:'/content'}}, {function:'fp::take', payload:{n:20000}}, {function:'state::set', payload:{scope,key}}]. Returns per-step sizes and a preview, not the value. shell::*/coder::* steps run under the session's harness-stamped filesystem scope; without one (no working directory, or a non-harness caller) they are refused — call them directly instead. Database write steps are refused only while `approval::gate` is registered.
Reverse an array (lodash _.reverse, immutable like lodash/fp): { value }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Count a collection (lodash _.size): array length, string chars, or object key count: { value }. Non-collections error instead of returning 0. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Sort array elements ascending by the value at a JSON pointer (lodash _.sortBy, stable): { value, path } — path "" sorts the elements themselves (primitives). Keys must all be numbers, strings, or booleans; an element missing the path errors. Pair with fp::reverse for descending. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Split a string into an array of strings (lodash _.split): { value, separator: "\n" }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Total an array of numbers (lodash _.sum/_.sumBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" } to pluck the addend from each element first. An empty array totals 0; a non-numeric element errors rather than being skipped. All-integer inputs total to an integer, so the result compares cleanly in a fp::when guard. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Keep the first n elements of an array or the first n characters of a string (lodash _.take): { value, n }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Deduplicate an array, keeping first occurrences (lodash _.uniq): { value }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Guard: test the value at a JSON pointer ({ value, path?, op, to? }; ops ==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, exists, not_empty; path defaults to the whole value; a pointer miss FAILS the guard, it never errors). Direct calls return { passed, value }. As a fp::pipe step, a passing guard threads the ORIGINAL value onward unchanged and a failing one STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step (e.g. state::set) runs only when the condition holds.
Aggregate durable model usage, function outcomes, and available trace/span observability. `complete` is true only after every session in the durable tree has reached a terminal turn.
Read the durable root-and-descendant session tree for one harness run.

Spawn a sub-agent in a child session (direct call only — never a trigger target). Fire-and-forget: returns { child_session_id, child_turn_id } immediately; the child's outcome reaches you only through whatever destination its task names. The child is a LEAF by default (no spawn/send/trigger registration); pass options.orchestrator: true to grant the orchestration surface, still capped by the caller's own policy. The task must include literal values for every required resource selector (for example `db: "primary"`). Omit child `max_turns` unless its budget covers discovery, contract lookup, work, and the deliverable.
Read the current turn status for a session.

Read-only: the trigger bindings a session owns (durable records) — subscription id, trigger type/config, delivery target (absent = notifies the owner), conditions, lifecycle, and fire count. In-turn agent calls may omit `session_id` (defaults to the calling session).

Tear down one trigger binding by subscription id: unregister the engine trigger AND delete the durable record (an engine-side unregister alone strands the owner's armed wake). `session_id` must name the binding's owner; in-turn agent calls may omit it (defaults to the calling session). A still-armed wake torn down this way notifies its parked owner.
Enqueue a message
Discard (purge) a single DLQ message by ID
Redrive all DLQ messages back to the main queue
Redrive a single DLQ message by ID back to the main queue
Define and start a durable named function queue
Internal: reload queue configuration from the authoritative store.
Read one catalog model by {provider, id}; null when the model is not registered.
List catalog models, optionally filtered by provider and/or a capability flag.
Check whether a model supports a capability flag (fails open for unknown models).
List registered providers with their configured/available status.
Read one session's metadata (null when unknown).
Read a single entry by id (null when unknown).
List sessions with pagination, ordering, and status/metadata filters.
Load the active path as messages with entry ids, oldest first; pagination and role filtering.

Run a command in the foreground and return its full output. Put the program name in `command` (string) and arguments in `args` (string[]) — do NOT pass argv as an array in `command`. `timeout_ms` is capped at the configured max; negative/fractional values fall back to the default. `target` defaults to the host; pass { kind: "sandbox", sandbox_id } to run in a microVM. Optional host-only `cwd` scopes this call to a directory (jail-confined exactly like shell::fs::* paths; escaping it is S215), optional `env` (object) sets per-call values for ANY key except PATH/IFS/HOME/LD_*/DYLD_* or other loader/lookup and interpreter-startup keys (those reject S210 unconditionally) — and optional host-only `stdin` (string) is written to the program's standard input (use it for `tee`, `patch`, or any stdin filter instead of a shell heredoc). cwd/env/stdin on a sandbox target reject S210. Backend errors return { code, message }; common: S216 host exec error, S300 VM boot failed, S200 in-VM failure. argv-parse and denylist rejections are plain-string messages naming the violation.

Spawn a command as a background job; returns { job_id, argv } immediately. Same payload as shell::exec (command + args, do NOT pass argv as an array), including the optional host-only `cwd` (jail-confined; escape is S215), `env` (any key except PATH/IFS/HOME/LD_*/DYLD_* or other loader/lookup and interpreter-startup keys, rejected unconditionally), and `stdin` (string written to the job's stdin); violations and cwd/env/stdin on a sandbox target reject with an S210 message. Poll with shell::status, terminate with shell::kill, list with shell::list. Host background jobs ignore the per-call timeout_ms and run until they exit or shell::kill terminates them; set the operator config `max_bg_timeout_ms` (0 = unbounded, the default) to force-kill a runaway job after that long. Spawn-time failures (argv-parse, denylist, cwd/env gating, spawn, concurrency cap) are plain-string messages naming the violation; once spawned, per-job failures surface through shell::status (the job record's status/stderr), not this call's return.

Change permissions. `mode` is an octal string like "0644". `uid`/`gid` optionally chown. `recursive: true` walks the tree (symlinks skipped). Returns { entries_changed, path, recursive }. Errors return { code, message }; common: S210 bad mode, S211 not found or not accessible, S215 jail escape.

Search file contents. `pattern` is a Rust regex (RE2-like). `recursive` defaults true. `include_glob`/`exclude_glob` filter paths. Returns { matches, truncated }. Errors return { code, message }; common: S217 bad regex, S215 jail escape. For token-budgeted search with context lines and noise filtering, prefer coder::search.

List directory contents. `path` is relative to the primary fs jail root (the first fs.host_roots entry) when set, otherwise absolute. `target` defaults to host; pass { kind: "sandbox", sandbox_id } to run in a microVM. Errors return { code, message }; common: S210 bad path, S211 not found or not accessible, S212 not a directory, S215 jail escape. For paginated or recursive listings with noise filtering, prefer coder::list-folder / coder::tree.

Create a directory. `mode` is an octal string like "0755". `parents: true` creates missing parents and is idempotent. Returns { created, path, already_existed }. Errors return { code, message }; common: S210 bad mode, S213 exists, S215 jail escape.

Move/rename a path. `overwrite: true` allows replacing an existing dst. Returns { moved, src, dst, overwrote }. Errors return { code, message }; common: S211 src not found or not accessible, S213 dst exists, S215 jail escape. To move several paths in one call, use coder::move (batched, per-entry errors).

Stream a file from a path — returns a ContentRef HANDLE (channel_id/access_key), NOT the file text. For reading TEXT files use coder::read-file instead: it returns the content inline (windowed, batched) with no channel. This function is for binary/streamed payloads; the response carries the ContentRef plus size/mode/mtime. Errors return { code, message }; common: S211 not found or not accessible, S212 path is a directory, S215 jail escape, S218 file exceeds max_read_bytes, S216 channel/IO error.

Remove a path. `recursive: true` is required to delete a non-empty directory. Returns { removed, path, was_present }. Errors return { code, message }; common: S211 not found or not accessible, S214 dir not empty (pass recursive), S215 jail escape. To remove several paths in one call, use coder::delete-file (batched, per-entry errors).

Find-and-replace across files. `pattern` is a Rust regex by default (set regex:false for a literal). Provide either `files` (explicit list) or `path` (+ recursive). Returns { results, total_replacements }. Errors return { code, message }; common: S217 bad regex, S211 not found or not accessible, S215 jail escape. For line-oriented edits with post-apply echoes (no re-read needed), prefer coder::update-file.

Stat a single path (jail-relative when fs.host_roots are set). Returns the entry's type, size, mode, and mtime. Errors return { code, message }; common: S211 not found or not accessible, S215 jail escape. coder::read-file with stat: true additionally reports total_lines.

Write a file. Simplest form: { path, content: "text" } — `content` as a plain STRING is written inline (host target only), no streaming channel needed. For large/streamed payloads or a sandbox target, pass `content` as a ContentRef { channel_id, access_key, direction } from a write stream channel you opened through the engine's streaming layer (inline strings reject S210 on a sandbox target). To write several files at once, pass `files: [{ path, content, mode?, parents? }, ...]` instead of the single-file fields (host target, inline content) — the response then carries per-file results in `files`. `mode` is octal (default "0644"); `parents: true` creates missing parents. Errors return { code, message }; common: S210 bad mode/payload or inline-on-sandbox, S211 not accessible, S215 jail escape, S218 payload exceeds max_write_bytes, S216 channel/IO error. For plain text files, coder::create-file (batched) avoids the streaming channel.
Terminate a running background job by job_id (the UUID from shell::exec_bg). Errors return { code, message }; common: S211 no such job, S216 kill/signal delivery failure.
List background jobs (running + recently completed). Takes no arguments.
Fetch the full record (status, exit_code, timing) of a background job by job_id. Errors return { code, message }; common: S211 no such job.
Console-only workspace picker control plane: list child directories under an existing host directory. Returns canonical paths and never returns files.
Console-only workspace picker control plane: return canonical host directory anchors that an operator can browse before choosing a per-session working directory.
Console-only workspace picker control plane: validate that `path` is an existing host directory and return its canonical path.

Fan-in gate: record one arrival against a barrier and answer the typed condition decision — `skip` until the expected set has arrived, then `allow` EXACTLY ONCE carrying every arrival's payload. Use as a binding condition so a coordinator wakes once when N producers finish instead of once per producer.

Reserve a PRIVATE state namespace for the calling worker: its scopes become invisible to public state::* and to trigger fan-out, and internal accessors `<functions_prefix>::state::{get, list, compare-and-set}` are registered. A worker may only claim the namespace matching its own worker name (engine-stamped caller identity). Idempotent; claims survive a state restart.

Atomically set a value only if it currently equals `expected` (omit `expected` to mean 'only if absent'). Returns { swapped, current } — on a miss, `current` is what is actually there, so a caller can recompute and retry. The primitive for counters, claims and any read-modify-write that two callers might race.
Delete a value from state
Get a value from state
Get a group from state
List all state groups
List the keys stored in a scope
Internal: reload state configuration from the authoritative store on change.
Set a value in state
Update a value in state
Delete a value from a stream
Get a value from a stream
List all items in a stream group
List all available stream with metadata
List all groups in a stream
Send a custom event to stream subscribers
Set a value in a stream
Atomically update a stream value with multiple operations

Fetch a URL over HTTP(S) and return the response as a structured envelope. Use this INSTEAD of `shell::exec` with curl for any HTTP request — it returns {ok, status, headers, body} as JSON, enforces size/timeout caps, and blocks private / cloud-metadata / link-local addresses server-side (SSRF guard; loopback is allowed by default for harness dev workflows). To READ A WEB PAGE, set `format: "markdown"` — HTML is converted to Markdown and images come back viewable (image responses in that mode return the image itself plus a text line, not the {ok,...} envelope). For JSON: pass `json: {...}` (auto-stringifies + sets content-type) and `response_format: "json"` (auto-parses response into the `json` field). Method is case-insensitive. On failure returns `{ok:false, error, message}` where `error` is one of: invalid_payload, invalid_url, blocked_host, timeout, too_many_redirects, transport_error. Branch on `error`, not on text.

Install a worker from a registry slug, an OCI image ref, or a LOCAL project directory (one containing an iii.worker.yaml). Call worker::schema to see each source shape, and worker::validate to dry-run an iii.worker.yaml before installing. LOCAL installs run the project directory LIVE and start a source watcher: code edits auto-restart the worker, so do NOT re-add after changing source files — re-add (force: true) only when iii.worker.yaml itself changes. Installs can outlive a bus invocation timeout and CONTINUE server-side — on timeout, poll worker::status instead of re-issuing (the project lock stays held until the in-flight install finishes).
Wipe worker artifacts
List installed workers
Read a worker's recent stdout/stderr log lines from the engine host. `tail` bounds lines per stream (default 100, max 1000).
Uninstall workers and clear their artifacts
Introspect request/response schemas for worker::* triggers. Optional `function_id` filters to a single trigger. Also serves the iii.worker.yaml manifest schema under the pseudo-id "iii.worker.yaml".
Start a configured worker

Install/runtime status for ONE worker: installed?, running?, pid, version, a sanitized recent log tail, and a next-step hint. THE poll target after worker::add { wait: false } or after an add/update call hit a bus timeout (the install keeps running server-side).
Stop a running worker

Reinstall REGISTRY-installed workers preserving config (re-resolves iii.lock pins). LOCAL-path workers are NOT touched by this: their source watcher already auto-restarts them on code edits; only an iii.worker.yaml change needs worker::add with force: true. Like worker::add, updates can outlive a bus timeout and continue server-side — poll worker::status.

Dry-run validation of an iii.worker.yaml WITHOUT installing anything. Pass `manifest` (inline YAML text) or `path` (host file/dir). Returns errors, unknown keys, deprecated keys, and warnings — author, validate, then worker::add.

The `engine::functions::list` with search "register_trigger" returned nothing. That's strange. The system prompt documents `engine::register_trigger` as a primitive. Maybe it's an engine function not listed by the search. Let me look at the registered triggers list and the engine's own functions. Maybe `engine::register_trigger` exists but the search filter doesn't find it. Let me try `engine::functions::list { search: "trigger" }` or check `engine::workers::list` to see which workers are connected, and `engine::workers::info`.

Actually, let me try searching for "engine::" prefix.
The register/unregister functions may live under the engine worker. Let me check the engine worker's function inventory and get contracts for the core functions I'll use.

functions.description: Fetch a URL over HTTP(S) and return the response as a structured envelope. Use this INSTEAD of `shell::exec` with curl for any HTTP request — it returns {ok, status, headers, body} as JSON, enforces size/timeout caps, and blocks private / cloud-metadata / link-local addresses server-side (SSRF guard; loopback is allowed by default for harness dev workflows). To READ A WEB PAGE, set `format: "markdown"` — HTML is converted to Markdown and images come back viewable (image responses in that mode return the image itself plus a text line, not the {ok,...} envelope). For JSON: pass `json: {...}` (auto-stringifies + sets content-type) and `response_format: "json"` (auto-parses response into the `json` field). Method is case-insensitive. On failure returns `{ok:false, error, message}` where `error` is one of: invalid_payload, invalid_url, blocked_host, timeout, too_many_redirects, transport_error. Branch on `error`, not on text.

ContentFilter.description: Content-filter request block. `query`, `threshold`, `threshold_type`, and `min_word_threshold` are optional; their default values are applied when the filter runs (see the content pipeline), not at deserialization.

body.description: Raw request body as a string. Prefer `json` for JSON payloads.

content_filter.description: Content filter: prunes boilerplate. When set, `body` holds the filtered output in the requested `format` (page-reading mode only).

excluded_tags.description: Tag names / selectors to drop before rendering (e.g. "nav", "footer").

follow_redirects.description: Follow 3xx redirects. Defaults to true. Each hop is re-checked against the SSRF blocklist.

format.description: Page-reading mode: "markdown" | "text" | "html". When set, a browser UA + format Accept header are used, HTML is transformed, and response_format is ignored (treated as "text").

include_links.description: Add `links: { internal, external }` to the envelope.

include_media.description: Add `media: { images, videos, audios }` to the envelope.

json.description: Structured JSON payload. When set, the handler stringifies it and forces `content-type: application/json`; wins over `body`.

max_bytes.description: Cap on response body bytes. Defaults to the worker ceiling for raw fetches, or 256 KiB in page-reading mode (`format` set).

method.description: HTTP method. Defaults to GET. Case-insensitive ("get" works).

response_format.description: How to return the body: "text" (default), "base64", or "json".

target_elements.description: CSS selectors (tl subset: tag/.class/#id). Restrict rendered content to these regions. Unmatched selectors are ignored.

timeout_ms.description: Per-request timeout in ms. Capped by the worker's max_timeout_ms.

response_schema.description: Typed schema for the `web::fetch` response envelope. The handler returns a raw `Value` (its shape is request-dependent), so this type exists only to publish a concrete response schema: the SDK would otherwise emit the permissive `AnyValue` schema, which the registry rejects. Every field is optional because no single response carries all of them — success carries `ok`/`status`/`headers`/`body`/…, the page-mode viewable-image variant carries `content`+`details`, and failures carry `ok=false`/`error`/`message`.
response_schema.title: FetchResponse

functions.description: Spawn a sub-agent in a child session (direct call only — never a trigger target). Fire-and-forget: returns { child_session_id, child_turn_id } immediately; the child's outcome reaches you only through whatever destination its task names. The child is a LEAF by default (no spawn/send/trigger registration); pass options.orchestrator: true to grant the orchestration surface, still capped by the caller's own policy. The task must include literal values for every required resource selector (for example `db: "primary"`). Omit child `max_turns` unless its budget covers discovery, contract lookup, work, and the deliverable.

AgentMessage.description: The canonical transcript message union. Untagged: the single-variant role tags disambiguate deserialization (assistant/function_result/custom are tried before user so their required fields gate the match).

oneOf.description: Opaque redacted thinking payload — replayed verbatim on the wire.

ExposeMode.description: How allowed functions reach the model (harness.md § Exposure modes).

FunctionPolicy.description: The fail-closed dispatch policy (harness.md § Functions). Absent on the send => every call denied (a plain chat loop).

MessageInput.description: `message` is either a plain string (sugar for a user text message) or a full `AgentMessage`.

Mode.description: Console / send operating mode — prepends a short paragraph before the shared identity prompt. `ask` is also structural: the turn's dispatch policy is capped at the configured default policy, never widened.

OutputContract.description: Free text by default; `json` constrains the final answer to a JSON value, validated against `schema` when supplied.

filesystem_root.description: Absolute filesystem root for the child turn (e.g. an isolated `worktree::create` checkout), written to the child's `metadata.fs_scope.root`. When set it overrides the inherited scope for this child; when absent the child inherits its direct parent's root unchanged.

functions.description: Intersected with the parent policy — narrow, never escalate. An `ask`-mode child is further capped at the configured default policy.

max_children.description: Fan-out guard for the child's own spawns.

max_output_tokens.description: Inherits the parent's ceiling unless explicitly narrowed/overridden.

max_turns.description: Capped at the parent's remaining turn budget. Omit unless a strict child-specific cap is required. It must cover discovery/contract calls plus every work call; very small values (for example 2-3) commonly strand the child before it can produce its deliverable.

max_validation_retries.description: Override the child's validation-retry budget (output contract AND `harness::hook::post-turn` deny re-prompts). Default: worker config.

orchestrator.description: Grant this child the orchestration surface. Default false: a spawned child is a LEAF — its policy gains deny globs for `harness::spawn`, `harness::send`, `engine::register_trigger`, `engine::unregister_trigger` and `engine::registered-triggers::*`, so it performs its assignment and updates shared state without spawning, messaging sessions, or touching trigger registrations. `true` skips those denies; the child still never exceeds its parent's policy.

output.description: The child's deliverable: text / json / json+schema.

system_prompt_strategy.description: How `system_prompt` combines with the built-in prompt: `override` replaces it; `enrich` (default) appends to it; `disabled` omits it.

SystemPromptStrategy.description: How a caller-supplied system prompt combines with the built-in identity prompt.

oneOf.description: Caller prompt replaces the built-in prompt verbatim.
Caller prompt is appended to the built-in identity prompt.
No system prompt is sent to the model.

parent_session_id.description: Display-only parent for the console session tree, used when there is no live parent turn (e.g. a console- or workflow-issued spawn). Writes `SessionMeta.metadata.parent_session_id` so the console nests this child; it does NOT grant policy inheritance or parent-call resolution. Ignored when the dispatcher injects a real parent link (an in-turn spawn).

session_id.description: Spawn into this session, creating it if it does not exist (e.g. a fork, or a pre-chosen id to filter `turn-completed` subscriptions on); default: create fresh. An in-turn spawn may reuse an EXISTING id only inside its own tree (itself, or a child it spawned) — anything else is refused as a cross-run id collision. The response reports `reused: true` on reuse.

task.description: The child's self-contained goal — its opening user message. Include every resolved required selector literally (for example `Use database db: "primary"`); the child cannot infer resources from the parent.

reused.description: The named session already existed and was reused — its prior transcript and parent linkage were retained (only possible with an explicit `session_id`).

functions.description: Fan-in gate: record one arrival against a barrier and answer the typed condition decision — `skip` until the expected set has arrived, then `allow` EXACTLY ONCE carrying every arrival's payload. Use as a binding condition so a coordinator wakes once when N producers finish instead of once per producer.

BarrierConfig.description: The caller-authored half: what this barrier is and how to read an arrival out of the event.

carry.description: JSON pointer into the event for the value to accumulate (default: the whole event).

expect.description: A count, or the exact set of arrival keys.

id.description: Barrier identity. Two bindings sharing an id share the barrier — that is how several predecessors feed one downstream.

key_from.description: JSON pointer into the event for the arrival key (default `/key`, the state event's own key). A missing pointer is an error, not a silent unnamed arrival: two arrivals that both resolve to nothing would collapse into one and the barrier would never complete.

Expect.description: What the barrier is waiting for: a COUNT, or a named set. A named set is stricter and better: it catches the arrival that was never going to come.

request_schema.description: The condition-contract envelope. `event` is the fired event; the rest of the envelope (binding, context) is accepted and ignored so the same function works as a condition and as a direct call.
request_schema.title: BarrierInput

response_schema.description: The typed decision a condition returns.
response_schema.title: Decision

content.text:
Now I have contracts for `state::set`, `state::get`, `web::fetch`, `harness::spawn`, and `state::barrier`.

I still need the contract for `engine::register_trigger` — the wake-only shape. The system prompt documents it, but let me fetch the contract to be precise:

`engine::register_trigger` — "Register a trigger that fires `function_id` directly, with `metadata` delivered to the handler as a distinct argument (not folded into the payload). Returns the trigger id (pass it to engine::unregister_trigger)."

Wait — that description says it fires `function_id` directly. But the system prompt says: "Wake me — omit `function_id`. The event arrives as a message in THIS session and starts a turn." So there must be a wake-only variant where function_id is omitted. Let me fetch the contract for `engine::register_trigger` to see the schema.

Also I'll need `engine::unregister_trigger` for removing the timer at the end. Let me get both contracts.

Let me also check the `state` trigger type more carefully. The config: { scope, key } — from the trigger info:
- `scope`: Only fire for writes in this scope (any scope when unset)
- `key`: Only fire for writes to this key (any key when unset)
- `condition_function_id`: Optional function evaluated per event

The task says:
1. Arm a one-shot state wake for key `article` — config: { scope: "e2e:research:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236", key: "article" }, once: true, label `article-ready:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236`.
2. Arm a one-shot state wake over the whole scope — config: { scope: "e2e:research:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236" } (no key), once: true, label `analysts-complete:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236`, gated with `state::barrier` condition: id `research:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236:analysts`, expect ["summary", "facts"], carry each event's new value.
3. Arm a one-shot timer deadline five minutes out — config: { in_ms: 300000 }, once: true (timer is inherently once; but let me pass once: true anyway or rely on the timer being one-shot), any non-empty label.

Wait, the task says "Every registration is wake-only: omit any function target." So for the state wakes and timer, omit function_id. That's the wake-me shape.

Now, for the barrier gating: "Gate it with the shipped named-set barrier using id `research:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236:analysts`, expecting exactly `summary` and `facts`, and carry each event's new value."

The `state::barrier` condition contract:
- `condition_config` (BarrierConfig): { id, expect: ["summary", "facts"], key_from: "/key" (default), carry: "/new_value" }
  - `id`: barrier identity
  - `expect`: the exact set of arrival keys — ["summary", "facts"]
  - `key_from`: default `/key` — the state event's own key. Good.
  - `carry`: JSON pointer into the event for the value to accumulate (default: whole event). The task says "carry each event's new value" → carry: "/new_value".

So the condition entry: { function_id: "state::barrier", config: { id: "research:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236:analysts", expect: ["summary", "facts"], carry: "/new_value" } }.

The conditions entry per the system prompt: `conditions: [{ function_id, config? }]`.

Now the `engine::register_trigger` schema. Let me fetch it. Also `engine::unregister_trigger`.

The state trigger config uses `scope` and `key` as optional fields. Also, does the "state" trigger type support `conditions`? The `engine::register_trigger` is the general registration; conditions are part of the register_trigger payload per the system prompt: `conditions: [{ function_id, config? }]`.

Let me fetch engine::register_trigger and engine::unregister_trigger contracts.

Also note: the trigger type "state" has a `condition_function_id` config field, but the system prompt says condition_function_id inside config is refused — it belongs to the engine's own contract (`conditions` array). So I'll use the top-level `conditions` array.

Let me fetch the contracts now.
I have the core contracts. Now let me fetch the trigger registration contracts and check existing bindings/state before arming anything.

functions.description: Subscribe the current harness session to a iii trigger: omit function_id to be notified in this session, or name a non-harness function to call with the event.

BindingTarget.description: What a fire dispatches. `function_id` is any iii function — `harness::send` for a wake or a sub-agent, anything else for a mechanical reaction.

event_into.description: JSON pointer where the event lands inside the payload (default `/event`).

payload.description: Payload template; the fired event is injected into it at `event_into`.

ConditionSpec.description: One declared condition. Evaluated at fire time with the typed decision contract; ordinary iii functions, so a barrier or a claim is just a function someone wrote.

LifecycleRequest.description: The caller-settable half of a binding's lifecycle.

expires_at.description: Wall-clock deadline (epoch ms) after which the binding stops.

max_fires.description: Lifetime delivery budget; the binding retires on its Nth delivery.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. The top-level `once` field remains accepted as shorthand.

conditions.description: Gates evaluated at fire time, in order, each an ordinary iii function answering `{ decision: "allow" | "skip", payload?, reason? }`. The built-in safety gates run first and are not listed here.

config.description: The trigger config, passed verbatim to the engine — e.g. `{ "expression": "0 */5 * * * *" }` for cron, or a `state` scope/key.

function_id.description: Target function called on each event. Omit for a notification message into this session — the only shape that can reach you. Any non-harness function your policy allows may be named; `harness::spawn` is NOT a binding target — a binding never starts an agent. Spawn children directly from a turn and register a wake on what they write.

label.description: A short human label echoed back in the notification text.

lifecycle.description: When the binding stops firing. `once` may also be given at the top level (the shorthand every prompt uses).

metadata.description: Call-binding template: `{ payload?, event_into? }`. `payload` is the fixed argument object sent to the target; `event_into` is a JSON pointer naming where the fired event is injected into that payload. Meaningless for a wake; sub-agent fields (task/model/session_id/ options) are rejected — spawning is not something a binding does.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. Defaults by SHAPE: a WAKE (no `function_id`) is once — it parks this session until the event; a CALL binding is STANDING — it runs per matching event until unregistered or its lifecycle ends; `cron` is recurring; `timer` is once. Pass `once` explicitly to override any of these.

target.description: Explicit target, the long form of `function_id` + `metadata`: `{ function_id, payload?, event_into? }`. The shorthands stay valid and mean exactly this.

trigger_type.description: The iii trigger type to listen on: `cron`, `state`, `stream`, `timer` (one-shot deadline: `{ "in_ms": <ms> }` or `{ "at": <epoch ms> }`), or another worker's custom trigger type (e.g. `database::row-changed`). For an ad-hoc signal, subscribe to `state` on a key and have the signaller call `state::set` on it (no dedicated emit needed — the engine fans the trigger out to every subscriber).

id.description: The id of the registered trigger; pass to `engine::unregister_trigger`.

functions.description: Remove a trigger subscription owned by the current harness session.

request_schema.description: Agent-facing unsubscribe contract. The id is the harness subscription id returned by [`SubscribeResponse`], not the underlying engine binding id.
request_schema.title: UnsubscribeArgs

removed.description: Whether a trigger with this id existed and was removed.

functions.description: List registered trigger instances (subscriber rows).

function_id.description: Exact function id match.

include_internal.description: Include rows whose target function is internal (`engine::*`). Defaults to false.

trigger_type.description: Exact trigger-type id match.

worker.description: Worker-name match against the worker owning the target function.

config.description: Full trigger config (e.g. `{ "api_path": "...", "http_method": "GET" }` for HTTP triggers, `{ "topic": "..." }` for events, etc.). Console list views need this structured payload to render method/path/topic. `config_summary` is a truncated display string and is kept for backward compatibility — do not parse it.

Good. The state scope is empty, and there are no session-owned bindings yet (the listed registered triggers are system bindings, not mine). 

Now let me register the three wake-only bindings:

1. **article-ready wake**: 
   - trigger_type: "state"
   - config: { scope: "e2e:research:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236", key: "article" }
   - label: "article-ready:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236"
   - once: true (wake defaults to once anyway, but pass explicitly)
   - No function_id (wake-only)

2. **analysts-complete barrier wake**:
   - trigger_type: "state"
   - config: { scope: "e2e:research:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236" } (whole scope, no key)
   - label: "analysts-complete:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236"
   - once: true
   - conditions: [{ function_id: "state::barrier", config: { id: "research:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236:analysts", expect: ["summary", "facts"], carry: "/new_value" } }]
   - No function_id (wake-only)

3. **timer deadline**:
   - trigger_type: "timer"
   - config: { in_ms: 300000 } (five minutes)
   - label: "deadline:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236" (any non-empty label)
   - No function_id (wake-only)

into.description: JSON pointer in THIS step's payload where the previous step's value lands (default `/value`). Object keys only (`~0`/`~1` escapes are decoded); indexing into arrays is unsupported.

payload.description: Base payload for the call.

preview_chars.description: Preview length of the final threaded value in the receipt (capped at 8000).

through.description: Steps run in order; step N+1 receives step N's threaded value.

chars.description: Size of the value threaded OUT of this step (chars of its string or serialized form).

note.description: Set when the threaded value REPLACED a non-null literal already in this step's payload at the `into` pointer — almost always an omitted `into` on a write step clobbering the value it meant to write.

short_circuited.description: True when a `fp::when` guard failed and stopped the pipe: the receipts end at the guard and NO later step ran. Absent (false) on a full run.

functions.description: Extract the single value at a JSON pointer (lodash _.get): { value, path: "/content" }. A miss names the keys that were available. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

path.description: JSON pointer selecting the value to return (e.g. `/content`).

value.description: Input value (a pipe lands the previous step's value here).

functions.description: Keep the first n elements of an array or the first n characters of a string (lodash _.take): { value, n }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

n.description: How many array elements / string characters to keep.

value.description: Input value (a pipe lands the previous step's value here).

Hmm, but hold on. Let me reconsider what "inline" means here. Maybe the design intent: the wake notification carries the article object as its new_value. The spawn task for each leaf embeds the article object JSON. Since the content is ~6000 chars, embedding it in the task would be a large but bounded payload.

Let me think about the actual mechanics of harness::spawn. The task is a string (or AgentMessage). The spawn request payload is sent through agent_trigger. If I include the full 6000-char content in the task string, that's a big payload but the engine handles it. The concern in the HARD RULE is about ME re-typing it — but I wouldn't be re-typing; I'd be copying the value from the notification/state.

Actually, the deeper issue: the notification I received IS truncated. So I need to get the full article object from somewhere. The natural place: state::get. But that brings 6000 chars into my context (the response). Then I'd have to reproduce it in the spawn payload — from my context — which means the model has to emit the full 6000 chars in the tool call arguments. That's the stall/death scenario.

Alternative: Is there a way to pass the article to the leaf WITHOUT it going through me? 

Hmm — what about having the leaf read from state? No — "They need no state read because the article payload is inline" and they're narrowed to "function discovery plus the single state-write capability" — they can't read state.

What about fp::pipe? harness::spawn is a "turn-control" step, excluded from pipes.

Hmm. Let me reconsider. Maybe the test's intent is genuinely to embed the article inline in the spawn task, and the truncation is just the notification display — the actual event in the session contains the full new_value. As the model, I received the notification text with truncation. So I don't have the full content verbatim in my context.

Wait, actually — maybe I should re-read the wake notification. The message ends with "…(truncated)". So I got only the beginning of the content. I cannot reconstruct the full 6000 chars from my context.

So to embed the full article inline in the spawn tasks, I MUST fetch it from state::get. That returns the full article object (6000+ chars). This is a direct call whose result I must read in full to re-emit — exactly the anti-pattern. BUT — the task REQUIRES the leaves to receive the article inline. The task is the spec; the HARD RULE is a general guideline to avoid stalls, but here the test explicitly designs for inline payloads. 

Hmm, let me weigh: The task says "receive the complete article object inline". It's unambiguous. And it says the leaves "need no state read because the article payload is inline". So the test expects the article (including content) to be in the spawn task.

Actually — wait. Maybe there's a smarter reading. The wake's new_value is delivered to me in the notification. Even though displayed truncated, perhaps the full value is available. But I can only act on what I can see/emit. I can't emit what I can't see.

Let me think about the mechanics differently. What if I embed the article object via a state::get inside... no, harness::spawn is direct-only, and the task text is what the child sees. There's no way for the spawn to pull from state without the child having read access.

OK here's another thought: maybe I should call state::get to get the full article, and then the spawn tasks reference... no wait.

Actually, let me reconsider the scale. 6000 chars of content + url + title. The full article object JSON is ~6400 chars. The spawn task text would be maybe 6.5-7k chars. That's a moderately large but not insane payload for a spawn call. The HARD RULE says bulk data "does not pass through you" and "Re-typing a big result into another call's arguments stalls the provider stream mid-call for minutes". 6000 chars is on the border. The rule is really about huge documents (100k+ chars). 6k chars is manageable — the example in the system prompt uses `fp::take { n: 20000 }` as a trim, suggesting even 20k is borderline-ok.

But the core problem remains: I have the article truncated in my context; I can't re-emit the full content. I need to get it from state.

Hmm wait, actually — let me re-read the notification once more:

"[notification] article-ready:...: {"_caller_worker_id":"...","event_type":"state:created","key":"article","new_value":{"content":"Cache replacement policies - Wikipedia\n\n[Jump to content](#bodyContent)\n\n Main menu\n\nMain menu\n\nmove to sidebar hide \n\nNavigation \n\n*   [Main page]... About Wik …(truncated)"

Yes, truncated. So the full content is not in my context.

Decision: I'll call state::get to retrieve the full article object. Then spawn the two leaves with the article inline. 

But the anti-pattern warning... Let me think about whether there's an alternative that satisfies "inline" AND avoids me holding 6000 chars in context.

Alternative: spawn the leaves with a task that says "read the article from state scope/key" — NO, leaves are narrowed to write-only state, no read. The task explicitly says they need no state read.

Alternative: Can I make the leaf task reference a file? No — leaves are narrowed to function discovery + state::set.

Hmm, wait. Actually — let me reconsider. Is the truncation of the notification a display-only artifact, and does the full payload actually exist in the conversation? In iii, wake notifications inject the event into the session as a message. The display might truncate, but the underlying message content is the full JSON. As the model, I see the truncated version. So no.

OK let me just accept: I need the full article from state. Actually — hold on. Let me reconsider whether I even need the CONTENT inline, or whether the leaves could get away with a shorter task.

The task spec for the SUMMARIZER leaf: "receive the complete article object inline, then write summary as { role: "summarizer", title: "<title>", bullets: [...] }". The bullets must contain five crisp non-empty points ABOUT THE ARTICLE. The summarizer needs the content to summarize. Similarly the fact-extractor needs the content for concrete facts.

So the content MUST reach the leaf. Options: (a) inline in task (spec's design), (b) leaf reads state (spec forbids — "They need no state read because the article payload is inline", and narrowed functions exclude state::get).

Given the spec is explicit, I'll go with (a): embed the full article object in each leaf's task. To do that, I need the full article from state::get.

Now — the "bulk through chat" concern. state::get returns the full article (~6400 chars JSON). That enters my context once. Then I emit two spawn calls each containing the article inline (~6400 chars each). That's the spec's design. The provider stream will have to emit ~13k chars of arguments. It might be slow but it's the required design. The HARD RULE's example threshold (20000) suggests 6k is acceptable-ish.

Hmm, wait. Actually, let me reconsider once more. Is there a way to do this WITHOUT the article content entering my context AND satisfying "receive the complete article object inline"?

What about... the spawn task could contain a reference like "the article object is at state scope/key" and the leaf... no, can't read.

What about passing the article via the task being a full AgentMessage with content blocks? Still needs the content in my emission.

I think the spec genuinely wants inline. The test was probably authored knowing the wake delivers the full new_value (in a non-truncated real scenario?) — but here it IS truncated. Hmm, OR the test expects me to read state::get and then inline it.

Actually — you know what, let me reconsider. Maybe the truncation is because the notification message in the harness has a size cap for display. But there's another possibility: the wake notification message content itself might be truncated server-side for very large events. Either way, I need state::get.

Wait, actually, let me reconsider AGAIN. There might be an even cleaner path that still honors "inline": 

The spawn `task` is a MessageInput (string or AgentMessage). What if the task references the article via... no.

OK. Decision made: state::get to retrieve the full article, then two spawns with the article embedded inline in each task.

Hmm, but hold on — will I be able to faithfully reproduce 6000 chars of content into the spawn payload? The model emits the tool call arguments. If I read the full content in the state::get response, I can include it in the next tool call arguments. It's going to be a very large emission (~13k chars total across two spawns). This is risky (stall) but it's what the spec demands. 

Actually, WAIT. Let me reconsider whether I can avoid re-emitting by using harness::spawn's task as a MessageInput with... no, the task text must contain the content.

Alternatively — think about this: could I spawn ONE leaf and have it... no, spec requires two parallel spawns.

Hmm, alternatively: could the spawn task embed the article via a state pointer AND the leaf's narrowed policy include state::get? The spec says: "Narrow each leaf to function discovery plus the single state-write capability. They need no state read because the article payload is inline". So the narrowed allow list = engine::functions::list, engine::functions::info, state::set. No state::get. The spec is explicit. Inline it is.

Let me now get the article from state. Actually — hmm, one more consideration: do I want to read the FULL article into context? state::get returns the whole stored value. ~6400 chars. Fine — it's needed to fulfill the spec.

Actually, let me think about whether I should pass the content at all... The summarizer needs to produce 5 bullets about cache replacement policies. It could arguably do that from just the title + first 400 chars? No — the spec says "receive the complete article object inline". Complete. I'll pass the complete article.

Let me call state::get for the article now.

Actually — wait. Let me reconsider the bulk-data rule one final time, because there's a real tension and I want to be careful:

HARD RULE: "bulk data does not pass through you. A value you will not personally reason about — a fetched document, a big function result, a list to reshape — moves worker→worker via fp::pipe, never through the chat."

The article (6000 chars) is a "fetched document" I will NOT personally reason about — I don't need to read it. The rule says move it worker→worker via fp::pipe, never through the chat.

But harness::spawn cannot be in a pipe ("Trigger-control, session/approval, credential/config, LLM-routing, and turn-control steps are excluded — call those directly"). And the spec explicitly demands inline.

So the spec overrides the general guideline here — it's an e2e test of exactly this flow: wake → inline spawn. The "article payload is inline" design is the point of the test. I'll follow the spec.

BUT — here's the practical question: how do I get the full article to embed? I have two sources:
1. state::get (brings it into my context, then I re-emit it in spawn args)
2. The wake notification (truncated — useless for full content)

So state::get it is. One read, then emit.

Hmm, actually, hold on. Let me reconsider — is there any chance the harness delivers the full wake payload and I should just use it? The message I received says "(truncated)" — so no.

Alright, executing: 
1. state::get { scope, key: "article" } → full article object.
2. harness::spawn summarizer with task containing the article inline.
3. harness::spawn fact-extractor with task containing the article inline.
4. End turn.

For the spawns, per the spec:
- Each leaf: narrowed to function discovery (engine::functions::list, engine::functions::info) + single state-write (state::set). 
- options: { functions: { allow: ["engine::functions::list", "engine::functions::info", "state::set"] } }
- session_id: I must name each child. "Name every child you spawn: always pass session_id." Choose short readable slugs + random chars. E.g. "summarizer-728a" and "facts-728a". Actually the session id is e2e_728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236 — the run's session id. I should derive a suffix from the unique session id. Let me use session ids like "summarizer-728aff" and "factextract-728aff" — hmm, "a short readable slug plus a few random characters". The session id is unique enough. I'll use "summarizer-a3f9" and "fact-extractor-b7c2" or similar. Let me pick: "summarizer-k2x8", "fact-extractor-m4q7". These are short readable slugs with random chars.

- The task must include:
  - The complete article object inline (verbatim: url, title, content).
  - The exact destination: scope "e2e:research:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236", key "summary" / "facts".
  - The exact output shape.
  - Instruction that it's a leaf: write the result, then end. No spawn, no trigger registration, no fetch.
  - It needs state::set contract: it will discover engine::functions::info for state::set? Actually it can just be told the function id and shape. But the child inherits policy + discovery functions, so it can fetch the contract itself. Give it the function id "state::set" and the literal scope/key.

Task for SUMMARIZER:
"Your job: produce a 5-bullet summary of the article below and persist it. Use the function state::set (discover its contract via engine::functions::info if needed; call it as `state::set` with scope "e2e:research:728aff6771934397aa566b35098cf236" and key "summary"). Write exactly this value:
{ "role": "summarizer", "title": "Cache replacement policies", "bullets": ["...", "...", "...", "...", "..."] }
with exactly five crisp, non-empty bullet points distilled from the article content. Then end your turn. Do not spawn, register triggers, fetch, or read state.

ARTICLE (complete object):
{ "url": "...", "title": "...", "content": "<6000 chars>" }"

Hmm — embedding the content inside the task string. The content is ~6000 chars of markdown with quotes, newlines, etc. I need to embed it as a JSON string within the task text, or as a JSON object. The task is a string. I'll embed the whole article as a JSON object literal within the task text, properly escaped... that's going to be painful with escaping. 

Alternative: keep it simple — embed the article as a fenced JSON block in the task text, e.g.:

ARTICLE JSON (verbatim, complete):
{"url":"...","title":"...","content":"Cache replacement policies - Wikipedia\n\n[Jump to content](#bodyContent)\n\n ..."}

But the content contains double quotes and backslashes (e.g. "Visit the main page [z]" with quotes, and markdown links like [Main page](/wiki/Main_Page "Visit the main page [z]")). Embedding raw markdown inside a JSON string requires escaping all double quotes and backslashes. That's heavy.

Better approach: don't wrap in JSON. Just give the raw content as a text block in the task:

"Here is the article content (raw markdown):
<raw 6000-char markdown>

Write ..."

The raw markdown contains double quotes, but since I'm not JSON-wrapping it inside the task string, that's fine — the task is just a text string. The spawn payload is { task: "..." } — a single string field. The content with newlines and quotes is fine as long as the task field is a valid JSON string (which the tool layer handles when I emit the payload object).

Hmm, but the agent_trigger payload is a JSON object — the task string will be JSON-encoded by me in the emission. Newlines in the content become \n in the JSON I emit. That's unavoidable and fine.

But here's the rub: I have to EMIT the full 6000-char content twice (once per spawn). That's the design. ~13k chars of emission. Risky for stalls but required.

Alternatively — could I make ONE spawn's task include the article, and the other reference it via state read? No — spec forbids state reads.

OK, let me also double check the exact bullets/facts requirements:
- Summarizer: exactly five crisp, non-empty points. bullets array of 5 strings.
- Fact-extractor: at least five concrete facts, algorithms, or figures. facts array with 5+ strings. "Include at least five concrete facts" — I'll ask for exactly five or "at least five"? The stored shape shows 5 entries; "at least five". I'll instruct five or more, but the example shows 5. To keep the merge auditable, exactly 5 is cleanest, but spec says "at least five" for facts. I'll say "at least five" and let the child decide (probably exactly 5). For bullets: "exactly five".

Now — the narrowed function policy: options.functions.allow = ["engine::functions::list", "engine::functions::info", "state::set"]. 

Wait — do the children need engine::functions::list AND engine::functions::info? The system prompt says: "Contract discovery is never lost to narrowing — every child keeps engine::functions::list and engine::functions::info". So they're always available; but the spec says "Narrow each leaf to function discovery plus the single state-write capability." So allow list = discovery functions + state::set. I'll include all three explicitly to be safe and match the spec.

Also options: mode? Default. orchestrator: false (default, leaf). max_turns: omit (per guidance, omit unless needed).

Session ids: must be unique per child. I'll use "summarizer-728aff" and "facts-728aff"? The instruction: "When YOU choose the name, use a short readable slug plus a few random characters, e.g. `fetch-headlines-b4k9`; a bare slug risks landing on an earlier run's session". So: "summarizer-x7k3" and "factextract-p9q2". Let me pick: summarizer-4t8w, factextract-2m5d. Fine.

Now, the big question remains: HOW do I get the article content into the task? I need state::get first. Let me call state::get and see the full content in my context. Then I emit the spawns.

Actually hmm, wait — one more idea to avoid holding the content: What if I DON'T read state, and instead reconstruct the task from... no, I can't — the content is truncated in my context and I can't fabricate 6000 chars of Wikipedia content.

So: state::get first. Then two spawns. Let me do state::get now.

Actually — let me reconsider whether the spawn tasks really need the FULL content or whether a reasonable interpretation is: "the complete article object inline" = the article object with its content. The content is what makes it "complete". Yes, full content.

One more consideration on emissions: after state::get, I'll have the full article in context. When I emit the two spawn payloads, I must include the content verbatim. The model will reproduce it. There's risk of transcription drift, but that's inherent to the design. The leaves will receive whatever I send; they summarize/extract from it. If I drift slightly, the content is still Wikipedia markdown and the leaves can still produce valid output. The url/title I'll keep exactly.

Alright — call state::get.

The `article-ready` wake arrived with the article's `new_value` (displayed truncated). I need the complete article object to embed inline in the leaf tasks, so let me pull the full stored value from state.

{"content":"Cache replacement policies - Wikipedia
